blocks.text: The patient's presentation episodic headaches, palpitations, sweating, pectus excavatum, high extremities-to-body ratio, tongue growth, and a flank mass are characteristic of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B). MEN 2B is an autosomal dominant genetic syndrome caused by a mutation in the RET proto-oncogene.

It is associated with the development of multiple endocrine tumors, such as medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid adenomas. MEN 2B is also characterized by distinctive physical features, including marfanoid habitus (high extremities-to-body ratio), mucosal neuromas (growth on the tongue), and gastrointestinal ganglioneuromas.
**Incorrect Options:**

items.text: **Option A - MEN 1:** MEN 1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1) is characterized by the development of tumors in multiple endocrine glands, including the parathyroid glands, pancreas, and pituitary gland. It does not typically present with the specific physical features described in the patient.

**Option B - MEN 2A:** MEN 2A is another form of multiple endocrine neoplasia caused by RET gene mutations. It is characterized by the development of medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism. The physical features associated with MEN 2B, such as marfanoid habitus and mucosal neuromas, are not typically seen in MEN 2A.

**Option D - Neurofibromatosis type 2:** Neurofibromatosis type 2 is a genetic disorder characterized by the development of bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) and other central nervous system tumors. It does not typically present with the specific physical features described in the patient.

blocks.text: Pheochromocytomas are tumors that arise from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, resulting in excessive production of catecholamines such as epinephrine and norepinephrine. These tumors can produce various hormones and vasoactive substances. They do not produce secretin. Secretin is a hormone produced by the S cells of the duodenum.
**Incorrect Options:** Options A, C, and D: Pheochromocytomas produce.

Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is a rare disorder characterized by the proliferation and accumulation of Langerhans cells, a type of immune cell, in various tissues. LCH can affect multiple organs, including the bone, skin, and lymph nodes. In the context of the given X-ray showing a punched-out lytic lesion in the cranium, LCH becomes a probable diagnosis.
**Incorrect options:**

items.text: **Option A. Multiple myeloma:** Multiple myeloma is a type of blood cancer that involves the abnormal proliferation of plasma cells, a type of white blood cell, in the bone marrow. Multiple myeloma is usually associated with abnormal hematological and urinary test results, which were reported as normal in this case.

**Option C. Metastasis:** Metastatic lesions can be seen in various organs, including the bone. However, the X-ray findings alone cannot definitively indicate metastasis. A detailed clinical history and further investigations, such as imaging studies and biopsy, are necessary to identify the primary tumor and confirm metastasis.

**Option D. Hyperparathyroidism:** Hyperparathyroidism is a condition characterized by excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) by the parathyroid glands, leading to high levels of calcium in the blood. While hyperparathyroidism can cause bone changes, such as osteopenia or osteoporosis, the typical X-ray appearance associated with hyperparathyroidism is not a punched-out lytic lesion.

blocks.text: Is the correct answer. It is a viral skin infection caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV). Molluscum contagiosum presents as skin-coloured or pearly umbilicated papules. Microscopically, it shows characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusions called molluscum bodies. These bodies consist of aggregates of viral particles surrounded by host cell reaction.
The given clinical presentation of skin-coloured umbilicated papules along with the provided microscopic image of molluscum bodies strongly suggests molluscum contagiosum.
**Incorrect Option:**

items.text: **Option A: Herpes virus.** Herpes virus infections typically present with grouped vesicles or ulcers and are associated with a burning or tingling sensation. The microscopic appearance of herpes virus infection would show multinucleated giant cells and intranuclear inclusions called Cowdry bodies. This description does not match the clinical and microscopic findings provided, so herpes virus is an incorrect option.

**Option B: Verruca vulgaris,** also known as common warts, is caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV). Verruca vulgaris presents as rough, hyperkeratotic papules with a characteristic cauliflower-like appearance. Microscopically, verruca vulgaris would show hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and presence of koilocytes (enlarged keratinocytes with perinuclear clearing). The given clinical presentation and microscopic image do not correspond to verruca vulgaris, so this option is incorrect.

**Option D: Lichen planus** is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by pruritic, polygonal, flat-topped papules. The microscopic findings in lichen planus include band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction, known as sawtooth appearance. Lichen planus is not associated with the clinical or microscopic features described in the case, so this option is incorrect.

blocks.text: Laminin is the most abundant glycoprotein found in basement membranes. It is a large protein complex composed of three different polypeptide chains (α, β, and γ) that form a cross-shaped structure. Laminin plays a crucial role in the structure and function of basement membranes, including cell adhesion, migration, and signalling.
**Incorrect Options:**

items.text: **Option A - Fibronectin:** Fibronectin is a glycoprotein present in the extracellular matrix and is not the most abundant glycoprotein in basement membranes.
**Option C - Integrin:** Integrins are cell surface receptors that mediate cell adhesion to the extracellular matrix but are not glycoproteins themselves.
**Option D - Syndecan:** Syndecan is a transmembrane heparan sulfate proteoglycan and is not the most abundant glycoprotein in basement membranes.

blocks.text: Tubulin is not an intermediate filament. It is a protein that polymerizes to form microtubules, which are involved in various cellular processes such as intracellular transport, cell division, and the maintenance of cell structure.
**Incorrect Options:**

items.text: **Option A - Vimentin:** Vimentin is an intermediate filament protein found in various types of cells, including mesenchymal cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells. It provides structural support to the cytoskeleton and helps maintain cell shape and integrity.

**Option C - Desmin:** Desmin is an intermediate filament protein primarily found in muscle cells, including skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle cells. It provides structural support to muscle fibers and plays a role in maintaining muscle integrity.

**Option D - Neurofilament:** Neurofilament is an intermediate filament protein specifically found in neurons. It contributes to the structural organization of neuronal axons and provides mechanical support to the axons, allowing for efficient signal transmission.

blocks.text: The presence of osteoclast-type giant cells with intralesional bone formation is seen in clear-cell chondrosarcoma.

**Chondrosarcoma:** Chondrosarcomas are malignant cartilage-producing tumours. The majority of them have mutations in IDH1 and IDH2 genes. It is the second most common malignant matrix-producing tumour of the bone.

items.text: **Age:** 40 years or older
**Sex:** Higher predominance in males

blocks.text: The clear cell and mesenchymal variants occur in younger people in their teens or 20s. Chondrosarcomas commonly arise in the axial skeleton, especially the pelvis, shoulder, and ribs. The popcorn/honey comb matrix is a finding in chondrosarcoma, characterized by irregular calcifications within the cartilage matrix. Histologically, they are classified into 4 types.

rows: Neoplastic cartilage infiltrates the marrow space and surrounds the pre-existing bony trabeculae.
Low-grade chondrosarcoma with a second, high-grade component that does not produce cartilage.
It contains sheets of large, malignant chondrocytes with abundant clear cytoplasm, numerous osteoclast-type giant cells, and intralesional bone formation.
Composed of islands of well-differentiated hyaline cartilage surrounded by sheets of primitive appearing small round cells.

blocks.text: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is a malignant tumour arising from skeletal muscle progenitors. It is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children and adolescents (Option 1). It commonly presents in the extremities (Option 3).
**Types:**

items.text: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma.
Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.
Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma.
Spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma.

blocks.text: The tumours are often large, soft, and infiltrative, with areas of necrosis and haemorrhage.
**Microscopy:** Small, round to spindle-shaped cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm, sometimes with a myxoid stroma are also seen.
**IHC Positive Markers:** Desmin, myogenin, MyoD1, and muscle-specific actin (Option 2).
Rhabdomyosarcoma has an aggressive clinical course and can metastasise, particularly to the lungs, bone marrow, and lymph nodes. The image below shows alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.

Leiomyoma, also known as a uterine fibroid, is a benign smooth muscle tumour that commonly occurs in the uterus. These tumors are composed of well-differentiated smooth muscle cells and are the most common benign tumours in women of reproductive age.

items.text: **Genetic Factors:** Mutations in MED12 gene.
**Hormonal Influence:** Estrogen and progesterone
**Appearance:** Leiomyomas are typically firm, well-circumscribed, round, and whorled masses.

blocks.text: **Location:** Leiomyomas can be found in various locations within the uterus:

items.text: **Intramural:** Within the uterine wall.
**Submucosal:** Beneath the lining of the uterine cavity.
**Subserosal:** Beneath the outer covering of the uterus.

blocks.text: **Cellular Structure:** Leiomyomas are composed of spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells arranged in interlacing fascicles.
**OTHER OPTIONS:**

items.text: **Option 1: Adenomyosis.** Typically presents with a uniformly enlarged, boggy uterus. Histologically shows endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, not just smooth muscle cells.

**Option 2: Leiomyosarcoma.** Rare malignant smooth muscle tumor. Histologically shows significant atypia, high mitotic rate, and areas of necrosis. Patients may present with rapidly growing mass and systemic symptoms.

**Option 3: Endometrial carcinoma.** Typically presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, especially postmenopausal bleeding. Histology shows malignant endometrial glandular cells, not smooth muscle cells.

blocks.text: **Liposarcoma:** Malignant adipose tissue tumour. Most common adult sarcoma. Typically occur in the sixth and seventh decades. Develop in proximal extremities and retroperitoneum.
**Three subtypes:**

items.text: **Well-differentiated:** chromosome 12 amplification, including p53 inhibitor MDM2.
**Myxoid:** t(12;16) translocation.
Pleomorphic

blocks.text: **Biopsy:**

items.text: **Well-differentiated:** Mature adipocytes with scattered atypical spindle cells.
**Myxoid:** Abundant basophilic extracellular matrix, arborizing capillaries ( chicken wire blood vessels ) and primitive fat cells ( lipoblasts ).
**Pleomorphic:** Sheets of anaplastic cells with bizarre nuclei and immature adipocytes, called lipoblasts.

blocks.text: **OTHER OPTIONS:**

items.text: **Option 1:** Lipoma is the most common benign soft tissue tumor of fat in adults and, upon biopsy, reveals mature fat cells with peripheral nuclei.
**Option 3:** Leiomyosarcomas are malignant, painless, firm masses arising from smooth muscle. These tumours are composed of eosinophilic spindle cells with blunt-ended, cigar shaped nuclei.
**Option 4:** Fibrosarcoma is a malignant tumour of fibroblasts with a \"herringbone\" architecture.

blocks.text: **Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (ABC):** Affects all age groups, with most cases in adolescence. Characterised by multiloculated blood-filled spaces (Option 1).

items.text: **Location:** Femur, tibia, and posterior vertebral body (Option 2).
**Genetics:** Chromosome 17p13 rearrangements result in fusion of the USP6 coding region in 70% cases. (Option 3) Highly expressed osteoblast genes like CDH11. USP6 upregulates NF-κB activity.

**Biopsy:** Blood-filled cystic spaces separated by thin, tan-white septa made up of spindle cells, osteoclast-like giant cells. Approximately one-third cases contain densely calcified, basophilic metaplastic matrix called blue bone (Option 4). Necrosis is uncommon.

blocks.text: A non-ossifying fibroma is the most likely diagnosis. A biopsy finding suggestive of storiform pattern made by benign spindle cells with scattered osteoclast-type giant cells.

**Non-Ossifying Fibroma:** Developmental defect in which fibrous connective tissue replaces bone. Age group: children and adolescents. Arise eccentrically in the metaphysis of the distal femur and proximal tibia.
Masses growing to 5 or 6 cm are classified as non-ossifying fibromas.
**Morphology:**

items.text: **Gross:** Yellow-brown.

**Microscopic:** Bland fibroblasts arranged in a storiform (pinwheel) pattern and macrophages with foamy cytoplasm or multinucleated giant cells with osteoblastic rimming. Hemosiderin is commonly present.

blocks.text: **Fibrous Dysplasia:** It is a benign childhood tumour caused by GNAS1 mutations, characterised by immature normal bone components and disorganised growth plates, linked to McCune- Albright syndrome. The components of normal bone are present, but do not differentiate into mature structure.
**Types:** Can be monostotic or polyostotic.

items.text: **Monostotic:** more common in craniofacial bones and femur.
**Polystotic:** commonly affected are pelvis, femur and tibia.

blocks.text: **McCuneAlbright Syndrome:** Commonly presented as precocious sexual development, mainly in girls. Polyostotic disease associated with café-au-lait skin pigmentations and endocrine abnormalities. Café-au-lait macules: dark large macules with irregular serpiginous borders on the same side of the body as the bone lesions.
**Mazabraud syndrome:** Fibrous dysplasia associated with soft tissue myxomas.
**Morphology:**

items.text: **Gross:** Tan-white, gritty structure.
**Nodules of hyaline cartilage:** disorganized growth plates.
Shepherd's crook deformity
**Microscopy:** Curvilinear trabeculae of woven bone that lack conspicuous osteoblastic rimming in a background of fibrous tissue ( Chinese letter pattern).

blocks.text: The clinical vignette, biopsy showing cords of epithelial cells, abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, vacuoles, and extracellular myxoid matrix is suggestive of chordoma.
Biopsy shows cords of epithelial cells, abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, vacuoles, and extracellular myxoid matrix.

**Chordoma:** It is a low-grade, slow-growing but locally invasive and locally aggressive tumour. They arise from the remnants of the notochord and occur along the midline spinal axis between the clivus and the sacrum, anterior to the spinal cord.
**Genetics:** Brachyury gene
**Morphology:**
**Microscopy:** Physaliferous cells (cells with bubbly or vacuolated appearance), abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, cords of epithelioid cells, vacuoles, and extracellular myxoid matrix.

The given clinical scenario suggests Ewing’s sarcoma. The correct statements regarding this condition are 2, 3, 4.

**Ewing’s sarcoma:** It is a malignant bone tumour characterised by primitive round cells without obvious differentiation. (Statement 1) Approximately 80% of patients are younger than 20 years of age.

Males are affected slightly more often than Females. (Statement 2) It usually arises in the diaphysis of long tubular bones, especially the femur and in the flat bones of the pelvis and presents as a painful, enlarging mass. The most common mutation (>90% of the cases) is t(11;22)(q24;q12). (Statement 3)
**Morphology:** The tumour is soft, tan-white, and frequently contains areas of haemorrhage and necrosis.

It comprises sheets of uniform, small, round cells with scant cytoplasm that may be clear due to abundant glycogen. Homer-Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes) are rounded cell clusters with a central fibrillary core, their presence indicates neuroectodermal differentiation. (Statement 4) Specific markers: CD99+ (MIC2) positive. Fibrous septae may also be present, but there is little stroma. Geographic necrosis may be prominent.
Chemotherapy-induced necrosis is a positive prognostic indicator. (Statement 5)
